newsitem.title: USA: US Southeast turns to incentives to lure industry.
newsitem.headline: US Southeast turns to incentives to lure industry.

text.p: Southeastern states are raising new revenues by using economic incentives to lure private industry and by switching to more creative financial management of existing funds, several state treasurers said Thursday.
The changes have been mandated by residents who are virulently opposed to any new taxes, the treasurers said at the Bond Buyer Southeast Public Finance Conference in Atlanta.
"Most of the taxpayers fell pretty much taxed out," Mississippi Treasurer Marshall Bennett said.

Mississippi now requires large businesses to make their monthly income tax payments via electronic transfer, getting the money into the treasury faster so it can begin earning interest sooner. Casinos, which have been a major boon to Mississippi's economy, must ante up even more quickly.
"We're making the casinos pay once a week so we get their money even faster," Bennett said.
Alabama is merging two oil lease revenue trust funds that have a combined principle of nearly $1.3 billion, and using the interest income to boost its general fund, state Treasurer Lucy Baxley said.
"One of the best sources of revenue we have is moving that money," Baxley said.
But with no more oil leases to sell, the state has also become "more aggressive than we've been in the history of the state" to lure new businesses.

Alabama was accused of starting a bidding war with neighboring states to attract the Mercedes-Benz plant that rolled its first recreational utility vehicle off the assembly line near Birmingham last week.

The state offered so many incentives that it was left scrambling two years ago to pay for them, finally arranging a private bond issue by a state pension fund to finance some of the perks, Baxley said.
"Obviously you can't do this over and over," Baxley said.

The Mercedes plant has already attracted a host of support industries, including auto parts makers. Those and other companies that move into the state will still get a 5 percent annual tax deduction each year for 20 years, Baxley said.
Even before a company moves into Georgia, the state starts training propsective workers to do the tasks that company will need, state treasurer Steve McCoy said.

The training program works in conjunction with Georgia's lottery-funded Hope Scholarship program, which allows any high school student with a B average or better to attend college or technical school.
"It's one of the strongest economic development tools that we have," McCoy said.
He said the end result is , "We are getting additional corporate income taxes we (otherwise) wouldn't get."
Mississippi and Tennessee use grants, low-cost loans and other financial aid to help local governments build road and water-sewer projects related to industrial development and expansion.
Those incentives helped lure the Saturn and Nissan plants that have strengthened Tennessee's economy, Treaasurer Steve Adams said.
Mississippi has used industrial development bonds to help finance child care centers for welfare recipients who are being nudged off the dole and into the workplace, Bennett said.

South Carolina has had "smashing success" by giving tax credits to companies that move their headquarters to the state and companies that operate subsidized child care programs. Two years ago, it created enterprize zones that give additional tax breaks to companies that move into depressed, rural areas.
Those incentives helped attract 26,000 new, high-paying jobs and $35 billion in new capital investment last year, Eckstrom said.
North Carolina Treasurer Harlan Boyles said creative financing will become even more important as the federal government shifts more responsibility to the states for Medicaid and welfare programs.

"States are epxected to do more with less. How do we fund all of these programs and expectations? New conditions are going to require new solutions," Boyles told investment bankers and financial advisers in the audience. "You're going to play a greater role in our future."
--Jane Sutton, 305-374-5013
